rpag-01-c1.text: M. R. P. McGuire. Pagan. New Catholic Encyclopedia (Encyclopedia.com).
rpag-01-c1.quote: It is significant, however, that the Christians did not adopt the term paganus in the meaning of non-Christian before the age of Constantine.
rpag-01-c1.claim: they did not use paganus for non-Christians before the age of Constantine

rpag-01-c1.text: James J. O'Donnell (1977). Paganus. Classical Folia 31.
rpag-01-c1.quote: These connoisseurs of the old religion were called 'hicks' behind their backs and, for deliberate and (I should think) devastating effect, to their faces in the heat of controversy
rpag-01-c1.claim: O'Donnell suggested the word carried a sneer: it let Christians call even rich, cultured senators "hicks" behind their backs.

rpag-01-c3.text: Marija Gimbutas (1987). Slavic Religion. Encyclopedia of Religion (Encyclopedia.com).
rpag-01-c3.quote: The descriptions that we have of Slavic idols and temples, it must be remembered, come from the writings of the very people who destroyed them.

rpag-02-c1.text: Mark Cartwright (2019). Hestia. World History Encyclopedia.
rpag-02-c1.quote: A birth ceremony involved carrying the baby around the hearth, brides and slaves new to the household were showered in nuts and figs before it
rpag-02-c1.claim: A newborn baby was carried around it, and brides and newly arrived slaves were showered with nuts and figs in front of it.

rpag-02-c2.text: Roman Inscriptions of Britain. RIB 143. Altar dedicated to Sulis. Roman Inscriptions of Britain.
rpag-02-c2.quote: To the goddess Sulis for the welfare and safety of Marcus Aufidius Maximus, centurion of the Sixth Legion Victrix, Aufidius Eutuches, his freedman, willingly and deservedly fulfilled his vow.
rpag-02-c2.claim: At Bath a freedman called Aufidius Eutuches set up such an altar to the goddess Sulis for the welfare and safety of his former master, a centurion of the Sixth Legion.

rpag-02-c3.text: Roman Inscriptions of Britain. A prayer to the goddess (Tab. Sulis). Roman Inscriptions of Britain.
rpag-02-c3.quote: The 130 tablets from Bath, many of them fragmentary or otherwise illegible, are one of the largest groups ever published.
rpag-02-c3.claim: recovered 130 tablets, one of the largest groups ever published

rpag-03-c1.text: Julius Caesar. "De Bello Gallico" and Other Commentaries. Project Gutenberg.
rpag-03-c1.quote: Nor do they regard it lawful to commit these to writing, though in almost all other matters, in their public and private transactions, they use Greek characters.
rpag-03-c1.claim: The druids thought it wrong to write their teachings down, although the Gauls used Greek letters for ordinary business.

rpag-03-c2.text: Mark Cartwright (2021). Druid. World History Encyclopedia.
rpag-03-c2.quote: A priest clad in white climbs the tree, cuts the mistletoe with a golden hook and catches it on a white cloak.
rpag-03-c2.claim: a priest in white climbs up, cuts the mistletoe with a golden hook

rpag-03-c3.text: English Heritage. Research on Stonehenge. English Heritage.
rpag-03-c3.quote: As the Druids were the only prehistoric British priests mentioned in the classical texts, he attributed Stonehenge to the Druids.
rpag-03-c3.claim: since the druids were the only prehistoric British priests named in classical texts, he credited them with Stonehenge

rpag-04-c1.text: John Fhær Engedal Nissen (2021). Research reveals recipe of Tollund man's last meal. Aarhus University.
rpag-04-c1.quote: As such, there is no sign of a severe food shortage that could explain why Tollund Man was sacrificed.
rpag-04-c1.claim: The meal was nutritious, so they found no sign of a famine that might explain a sacrifice.

rpag-04-c2.claim: He had taken blows to the head and the back, had been garrotted with a thin cord, and had his throat cut.

rpag-04-c3.claim: Chadwick has asked whether rubbish disposal and deliberate placing can be told apart at all

rpag-05-c1.text: Richard North (2005). Paganism, Anglo-Saxon. Encyclopedia of Religion (Encyclopedia.com).

rpag-05-c1.claim: suggests that Tacitus may have mistaken a divine husband and wife for a single earth goddess

rpag-05-c2.text: Richard North (2005). Paganism, Anglo-Saxon. Encyclopedia of Religion (Encyclopedia.com).
rpag-05-c2.quote: it looks as if Bede deified eostre on analogy with Februus, an invented Roman god whom he knew to be associated with the month of February
rpag-05-c2.claim: argues that Bede may have turned a seasonal word into a deity by analogy with Februus, a Roman god Bede knew to be associated with February

rpag-05-c3.claim: destroy the idols but keep the temples

rpag-06-c1.claim: twelve men were appointed to beat him with sticks, not because the wood could feel it, the Chronicle explains, but to insult the demon who had deceived people in that form

rpag-06-c2.text: Marija Gimbutas (1987). Slavic Religion. Encyclopedia of Religion (Encyclopedia.com).

rpag-06-c2.claim: In 1168 Christian Danes stormed Rügen and destroyed it.

rpag-06-c3.text: Law Library of Congress (2022). Return of a Sámi Drum. In Custodia Legis, The Library of Congress.
rpag-06-c3.quote: The use of Sámi drums was classified as witchcraft and criminalized, punishable by death, by the Danish King Christian IV in a 1609 proclamation
rpag-06-c3.claim: In 1609 King Christian IV of Denmark and Norway made drum use a crime punishable by death.

rpag-07-c1.text: Caroline Roope (2021). Where did maypole dancing originate?. Who Do You Think You Are? Magazine.

rpag-07-c1.claim: the first documented maypole with plaited ribbons appeared on a stage
